title: HCFM: Helmholtz Component Flow Matching for Time Series Anomaly Detection

paper.title: HCFM: Helmholtz Component Flow Matching for Time Series Anomaly Detection
paper.abstract: Abstract Flow Matching (FM) is an efficient simulation-free approach for training flow-based generative models, making it a promising foundation for scalable time-series anomaly detection (TSAD). However, standard FM learns a monolithic vector field in which nominal transport and local density-changing behavior are entangled. This creates a central challenge for TSAD; local expansion and contraction carry crucial anomaly-sensitive information, yet isolating this signal requires expensive Jacobian-trace estimation over the entire field. We propose Helmholtz Component Flow Matching (HCFM), an unsupervised TSAD framework that parameterizes the vector field prediction network with separate transport, compression, and residual heads. The transport head is constrained to be divergence-free, so divergence estimation is restricted to the compression head, while a lightweight residual head absorbs the remaining mismatch. This structured parameterization improves scalability and detection performance by separating volume-preserving nominal transport from density-changing compression, yielding cleaner anomaly signals from distinct deviations of nominal behavior. Experiments on large-scale univariate and multivariate TSAD benchmarks show that HCFM consistently improves detection accuracy while maintaining efficient inference compared with 16 baselines. The code is available at https://github.com/TrustAIoT/HCFM__time-series-anomaly/

sections.heading: I Introduction
sections.text: Time-series anomaly detection (TSAD) is commonly formulated as a one-class learning problem: a model is trained on nominal data and later scores future windows according to their deviation from learned normal behavior. This setting arises in industrial monitoring, cyber-physical systems, server telemetry, medical signals, spacecraft data, and other domains where anomalies are rare, costly, and difficult to label. Many deep TSAD methods therefore model nominality through reconstruction error, prediction error, likelihood, or latent-space distance [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 ] . A key challenge is that anomalies are not always expressed as large point-level error. Abnormal windows may instead appear through localized structural changes: suppressed variation, abnormal amplitude expansion, distorted morphology, or regime shifts that alter how nearby samples are distributed [ 6 , 7 ] . Such effects suggest that useful anomaly evidence may lie not only in how far a window is from nominal behavior, but also in how the learned nominal model locally deforms around it. However, most generative TSAD methods collapse these effects into a single reconstruction error, likelihood, or distance score, making it difficult to isolate the specific source of abnormality [ 5 ] . Flow Matching (FM) provides an appealing foundation for scalable TSAD. FM learns a vector field that transports samples from a simple base distribution to the data distribution using an efficient simulation-free objective [ 8 ] . This gives FM several practical advantages over common generative TSAD approaches: it avoids decoder reconstruction as the sole scoring mechanism, does not require iterative diffusion-style denoising, and does not impose the invertibility constraints of normalizing flows. These properties make FM attractive for efficient generative modeling of nominal time-series windows. However, standard FM predicts the vector field with a monolithic network, so nominal transport and local density-changing behavior are entangled in a single output. Divergence measures local expansion or contraction of the learned flow, and can therefore reveal anomaly-sensitive deformation around abnormal windows. Yet extracting this signal from standard FM requires estimating the Jacobian trace over the entire predicted field, which is computationally expensive and does not distinguish volume-preserving movement from density-changing behavior. Recent divergence-regularized FM methods, such as Flow Divergence Matching (FDM) [ 9 ] , recognize the importance of divergence by encouraging the learned field to better match the divergence of the target probability path. Nevertheless, FDM still applies divergence matching to a monolithic field predictor, so nominal transport and local expansion or contraction remain entangled in its output. We propose Helmholtz Component Flow Matching (HCFM), an unsupervised TSAD framework that parameterizes the FM field prediction with transport, compression, and residual heads. HCFM does not train separate flow models; rather, it predicts a single total vector field through an additive head structure. The transport head is constrained to be divergence-free, encouraging it to represent volume-preserving nominal movement. The compression head captures density-changing behavior through divergence, so divergence estimation is required only for this head rather than for the full predicted field. A lightweight residual head absorbs residual mismatch without dominating the transport and compression heads. Figure 1 illustrates the key idea. Standard FM uses a monolithic field that entangles nominal transport with local density-changing behavior. HCFM preserves a single final field but structures it into divergence-free transport, density-changing compression, and lightweight residual components. This component-structured parameterization localizes divergence-sensitive behavior to the compression head rather than the full field, preserving FM efficiency while exposing more interpretable anomaly evidence. We evaluate HCFM on large-scale univariate and multivariate TSAD benchmarks, including 250 UCR anomaly datasets and six multivariate datasets. Across these settings, HCFM improves over 16 representative baselines. On UCR, HCFM achieves a 10.4% relative best-F1 improvement over the best non-HCFM baseline, while on multivariate benchmarks it obtains the best aggregate results and the best per-dataset VUS-PR and best F1 on five of six datasets. HCFM also improves inference efficiency over monolithic divergence-based Flow Matching, reducing latency by 35% relative to FDM. These results show that component-structured Flow Matching yields more informative anomaly scores while maintaining efficient inference. In summary, our contributions are as follows: • Identify a structural limitation of monolithic Flow Matching for TSAD: nominal transport and local density-changing behavior are entangled in the learned vector field, making divergence-based anomaly evidence difficult to isolate. • Introduce HCFM, a component-structured Flow Matching framework that represents one final vector field through divergence-free transport, density-changing compression, and lightweight residual components, while retaining standard FM supervision. • Develop component-specific divergence scoring that localizes Jacobian-trace estimation to the compression component and combines this signal with reverse-flow base energy, yielding complementary evidence for different anomaly modes. • Establish the effectiveness and efficiency of the proposed structure through large-scale experiments on 250 UCR datasets and six multivariate benchmarks, including controlled ablations that isolate the contribution of field structure, divergence source, and residual allocation. • Open source code for reproducibility available at https://github.com/TrustAIoT/HCFM__time-series-anomaly/ Fig. 1: Motivating illustration of HCFM. (a) In standard Flow Matching, a monolithic predicted field entangles nominal transport with local density-changing behavior, producing an entangled divergence signal that bends otherwise clean transport paths. (b) The transport head in HCFM is constrained to be divergence-free, encouraging volume-preserving nominal movement without local expansion or contraction. (c) HCFM predicts a single final vector field through additive transport, compression, and residual heads, v θ = v T + v C + v R v_{\theta}=v_{T}+v_{C}+v_{R} . This structured parameterization preserves a clean transport backbone while localizing density-changing behavior to the compression component and using the residual head to absorb residual mismatch.

sections.heading: II-A Time-Series Anomaly Detection
sections.text: Time-series anomaly detection (TSAD) spans industrial monitoring, cyber-physical systems, cloud infrastructure, healthcare, spacecraft telemetry, and scientific sensing. Classical approaches include statistical process control, autoregressive modeling, change-point detection, distance-based subsequence analysis, and matrix-profile methods [ 10 , 1 ] ; deep methods instead learn nominal temporal structure with recurrent, convolutional, graph-based, attention-based, and Transformer architectures [ 3 , 11 , 2 , 4 ] . Many deep detectors score by reconstruction or prediction error [ 3 , 12 , 11 , 4 ] , yet expressive decoders can reconstruct anomalies well and limited models over-penalize uncommon but valid nominal patterns. Anomaly Transformer [ 2 ] and TranAD [ 4 ] improve long-range dependency modeling, but stronger sequence modeling does not by itself distinguish global deviation, local expansion or contraction, and residual mismatch, which HCFM separates by structuring the generative vector-field predictor.

sections.heading: II-B Generative Models and Flow Matching
sections.text: Generative detectors model nominal data and score deviations by likelihood, reconstruction, latent-space statistics, or transport. VAEs, GANs, normalizing flows, diffusion models, and score-based models have all been applied [ 13 , 14 , 15 , 16 , 17 , 5 ] , each with a characteristic tradeoff: VAEs and autoencoders inherit decoder-driven scoring artifacts [ 18 ] , GANs suffer mode collapse and training instability [ 19 ] , normalizing flows restrict architectures to maintain invertibility and tractable Jacobian determinants [ 20 ] , and diffusion models require iterative denoising or sampling. Flow Matching (FM) learns a vector field that transports a simple base distribution to the data distribution [ 8 , 21 ] , avoiding invertibility constraints, iterative diffusion-style denoising, and sole reliance on reconstruction. Standard FM, however, predicts the field with a monolithic output that couples nominal transport with local density change, making expansion or contraction difficult to isolate as an anomaly signal. Recent time-series FM work includes TSFlow [ 22 ] , which adapts FM to probabilistic forecasting using Gaussian-process priors and optimal-transport couplings. Closer to our setting, SGFM [ 23 ] applies conditional FM to TSAD with state-space sequence modeling, but still predicts a monolithic field. HCFM instead structures the learned vector field itself into transport, compression, and residual components, so that volume-preserving transport and density-changing behavior provide distinct anomaly signals.

sections.heading: II-C Divergence Matching and Divergence-Free Flows
sections.text: Divergence measures the local expansion or contraction of a continuous-time vector field and governs density evolution along the flow. Flow Divergence Matching (FDM) [ 9 ] trains the field to match both the target vector field and the divergence of the target probability path, addressing density information that directional matching alone may not capture. However, FDM retains a monolithic field in which transport and density change remain coupled. Divergence-free continuous flows [ 24 ] are volume-preserving normalizing flows: zero divergence gives incompressible dynamics with unit Jacobian determinant magnitude and simplifies quantities such as differential entropy, but constraining the entire flow prevents it from modeling arbitrary density changes. HCFM instead predicts a single FM field through additive heads and applies the constraint selectively: a divergence-free transport head preserves volume, a compression head captures density change and supplies component-specific divergence as anomaly evidence, and a residual head absorbs the remaining mismatch.

sections.heading: II-D Positioning of This Work
sections.text: HCFM differs from prior FM-based TSAD primarily in how the vector field is parameterized and diagnosed. It retains a single final field and standard FM supervision, but separates divergence-free transport, density-changing compression, and residual mismatch. Relative to standard FM, it exposes expansion and contraction through a dedicated compression component; relative to FDM, it localizes divergence scoring to that component; and unlike fully divergence-free flows, it preserves density-changing capacity in the overall model. Thus, HCFM provides a component-structured parameterization of Flow Matching for separating nominal transport from density-changing behavior and enabling targeted derivative-based diagnostics. Fig. 2: Architecture of Helmholtz Component Flow Matching (HCFM). HCFM trains a data-space Flow Matching model over interpolated time-series windows and replaces a monolithic vector-field predictor with additive transport, compression, and residual heads. The transport head captures divergence-free nominal movement, the compression head provides localized density-changing evidence through component-specific divergence, and the residual head absorbs remaining mismatch while being kept lightweight. Training supervises the combined final field and uses residual-energy and orthogonality regularization to shape the internal component allocation. At inference, HCFM combines base-energy and compression-divergence for anomaly detection and localization.

sections.heading: III-E Inference and Anomaly Scoring
sections.text: After training on nominal windows, HCFM scores each test window using two signals: reverse-flow consistency with the Gaussian base distribution and compression-head divergence along the learned trajectory. Given a test window x 1 x_{1} , we integrate the learned field backward from t = 1 t=1 to t = 0 t=0 , obtaining a base-space endpoint x ^ 0 \hat{x}_{0} and trajectory states { ( x t k , t k ) } k = 1 K \{(x_{t_{k}},t_{k})\}_{k=1}^{K} . Since nominal windows should map to typical samples under the base distribution, we define the base-energy score as s base ​ ( x 1 ) = 1 2 ​ ‖ x ^ 0 ‖ 2 2 . s_{\mathrm{base}}(x_{1})=\frac{1}{2}\|\hat{x}_{0}\|_{2}^{2}. The second signal is the divergence of the compression head. At each trajectory state, we estimate d C ​ ( x t k , t k ) = ∇ x ⋅ v C ​ ( x t k , t k ) d_{C}(x_{t_{k}},t_{k})=\nabla_{x}\cdot v_{C}(x_{t_{k}},t_{k}) using Hutchinson trace estimation. Unlike full-field divergence scoring, this only evaluates the compression component, which is the head explicitly designed to capture local expansion and contraction. We aggregate the compression divergence along the trajectory: s div ​ ( x 1 ) = 1 K ​ ∑ k = 1 K d C ​ ( x t k , t k ) . s_{\mathrm{div}}(x_{1})=\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}d_{C}(x_{t_{k}},t_{k}). The main HCFM score combines base consistency with compression-divergence evidence: s HCFM ​ ( x 1 ) = s base ​ ( x 1 ) + s div ​ ( x 1 ) . s_{\mathrm{HCFM}}(x_{1})=s_{\mathrm{base}}(x_{1})+s_{\mathrm{div}}(x_{1}). For timestamp-level evaluation, window scores are projected back to individual timestamps by averaging the scores of all windows covering each timestamp.

sections.heading: III-F Computational Complexity
sections.text: HCFM reduces the cost of divergence-based scoring by avoiding Jacobian tracing over the full learned vector field. Let K K denote the number of reverse-flow solver steps, P P the number of Hutchinson probes, and 𝒞 v \mathcal{C}_{v} the cost of one monolithic vector-field evaluation. Jacobian-free FM scoring only integrates the reverse ODE and computes the base energy, resulting in O ⁡ ( K ​ 𝒞 v ) O(K\mathcal{C}_{v}) inference time. Although efficient, this score does not explicitly capture local density-change information. Monolithic divergence-based scoring, including FDM-style scoring, additionally estimates ∇ ⋅ v θ \nabla\!\cdot v_{\theta} over the full vector field. With Hutchinson trace estimation, this gives O ⁡ ( K ​ 𝒞 v + K ​ P ​ 𝒞 v J ) O(K\mathcal{C}_{v}+KP\mathcal{C}^{J}_{v}) time, where 𝒞 v J \mathcal{C}^{J}_{v} is the cost of a Jacobian-vector or vector-Jacobian product through the full predictor. The derivative computation is therefore applied to the entire field, including components that may primarily model nominal transport rather than anomaly-relevant density change. HCFM uses the same reverse-flow integration but restricts divergence scoring to the compression component. v T v_{T} is divergence-free by construction, v C v_{C} captures local compression and expansion, and v R v_{R} absorbs residual mismatch. The resulting inference cost is O ⁡ ( K ⁡ ( 𝒞 T + 𝒞 C + 𝒞 R ) + K ​ P ​ 𝒞 C J ) O(K(\mathcal{C}_{T}+\mathcal{C}_{C}+\mathcal{C}_{R})+KP\mathcal{C}^{J}_{C}) , where 𝒞 C J \mathcal{C}^{J}_{C} is the derivative cost of the compression head. Thus, HCFM preserves divergence-aware scoring while replacing full-field Jacobian tracing with component-specific derivative estimation. Figure 3 summarizes this allocation. HCFM is matched to the monolithic predictor in total parameter count, so the comparison does not rely on increased model capacity. However, divergence is evaluated only on the compression component. In this configuration, v C v_{C} contains 37.6 % 37.6\% of the predictor parameters, so HCFM traces a 0.376 × 0.376\times derivative target, corresponding to 62.4 % 62.4\% fewer traced parameters than full-field divergence. sections.heading: Univariate benchmark.
sections.text: For the univariate setting, we use the UCR Time Series Anomaly Archive [ 25 ] . The UCR benchmark contains 250 curated time series from diverse real-world domains. Each dataset consists of a nominal training segment and a test segment containing an annotated anomalous interval. The benchmark includes point, contextual, and collective anomaly patterns, making it a challenging testbed for one-class TSAD. Prior work has noted that many TSAD benchmarks contain annotation errors, trivial anomalies, or unrealistic anomaly densities [ 26 ] ; UCR was designed to mitigate many of these issues and provides a more reliable evaluation environment.

sections.heading: Multivariate benchmarks.
sections.text: For the multivariate setting, we use six widely adopted real-world TSAD benchmarks. SMAP and MSL contain spacecraft telemetry from NASA missions [ 1 ] ; PSM and SMD contain server and infrastructure monitoring signals [ 27 , 3 ] ; GECCO contains water-quality measurements from a distribution monitoring system [ 28 ] ; and SWAN contains space-weather monitoring signals [ 29 ] . These datasets contain multichannel time series with ground-truth anomaly intervals and cover diverse operational conditions, anomaly densities, and inter-channel dependencies.

sections.heading: IV-B Baselines and Variants
sections.text: We compare HCFM against representative reconstruction-based, Transformer-based, diffusion-based, contrastive, and flow-based baselines. For reconstruction-based detection, we compare against established baselines such as LSTM-AE, DENSE-AE, LSTM-DT, USAD [ 11 ] , OmniAnomaly [ 3 ] , DONUT [ 30 ] , TadGAN [ 12 ] , and TSI-GAN [ 18 ] , where applicable. We additionally include MERLIN [ 31 ] , a discord-based time-series anomaly detection baseline. For Transformer-based detection, we include TranAD [ 4 ] and Anomaly Transformer [ 2 ] . We also compare against recent diffusion- and contrastive-learning baselines, including DiffAD [ 32 ] , ImDiffusion [ 33 ] , DCDetector [ 34 ] , and CARLA [ 35 ] . For flow-based baselines, we include vanilla data-space Flow Matching, Flow Divergence Matching (FDM), and SGFM [ 23 ] . Vanilla FM uses the same data-space Conditional Flow Matching objective as HCFM, but predicts the vector field with a monolithic network. FDM incorporates divergence information into a monolithic FM predictor. SGFM is a recent Flow-Matching-based TSAD method that combines conditional Flow Matching with state-space sequence modeling. These baselines isolate whether HCFM’s gains arise from Flow Matching itself, from divergence information alone, from sequence-modeling improvements in prior FM-based TSAD, or from the proposed component-wise field parameterization. For HCFM, the final model uses the transport, compression, and residual heads described in Sec. III-C . The main score family combines reverse-flow base energy with compression-head divergence. We also evaluate score variants based on transport energy, compression energy, residual energy, centered compression divergence, full-divergence diagnostics, and smoothed score transformations. sections.heading: IV-C Evaluation Metrics
sections.text: We evaluate anomaly detection using ranking-based, tolerance-aware, and thresholded metrics. Unless otherwise stated, metrics are computed at the timestamp level after projecting window scores back to timestamps using mean-overlap aggregation. For ranking-based metrics, we report AUROC and AUPRC/AP, where AUPRC is computed as average precision (AP). AUPRC/AP is especially informative for imbalanced TSAD benchmarks because anomalous timestamps are typically rare. We also report VUS-PR, which extends precision–recall evaluation by incorporating temporal tolerance around anomaly intervals. We use a VUS-PR sliding tolerance window of W = 64 W=64 timestamps, matching the time-series window length used during preprocessing. For thresholded metrics, we report best F1, precision, FP@95R, and Hundman F1 where applicable. Best F1 is the maximum timestamp-level F1 over all score thresholds, and precision is reported at the same operating point. FP@95R reports the false-positive rate at the threshold required to achieve 95% recall. For Hundman F1, predicted anomalous timestamps are grouped into contiguous intervals. A predicted interval is counted as a true positive if it overlaps any ground-truth anomaly interval; otherwise, it is counted as a false positive. Ground-truth intervals with no overlapping prediction are counted as false negatives, and F1 is computed from these interval-level counts. The reported tables use these metrics as follows. For UCR, we report best F1, precision, VUS-PR, AUROC, AUPRC/AP, FP@95R, and Hundman F1. For multivariate per-dataset results, we report VUS-PR and best F1. For aggregate multivariate results, we report AUROC, AUPRC/AP, FP@95R, and Hundman F1. Aggregate multivariate results are computed by averaging each metric across the six datasets.

sections.heading: IV-D Implementation Details
sections.text: For HCFM, we use overlapping windows of length W = 64 W=64 with stride one across datasets; this fixed setting is not imposed on all baselines, which retain authors’ recommended window settings when available. Each channel is standardized using training-only statistics, and the same transformation is applied to the test sequence. HCFM is trained in data space using the linear interpolation path described in Sec. III-B . Table I summarizes the HCFM architecture and training hyperparameters. All Flow Matching variants use matched preprocessing, training budget, and reverse-integration settings wherever applicable. The transport head uses a low-rank skew-symmetric parameterization, the compression head uses a scalar-potential Conv1D network with residual Conv1D blocks and SiLU activations, and the residual head uses a lightweight time-conditioned Conv1D field. The residual head is downweighted in the combined vector field and regularized using the residual-energy penalty and orthogonality loss described in Sec. III-D . During inference, test windows are reverse-integrated through the learned field to obtain base-space endpoints and trajectory states. HCFM computes base-energy and compression-divergence scores along this trajectory. Compression divergence is estimated only for the compression head using Hutchinson trace estimation, avoiding full-field Jacobian-trace scoring.

sections.heading: IV-E Window-Size Sensitivity
sections.text: We additionally evaluate HCFM with W ∈ { 16 , 32 , 64 , 128 } W\in\{16,32,64,128\} across 15 UCR datasets while keeping the remaining protocol fixed. Relative to W = 64 W=64 , mean Best F1 is approximately 30% lower at W = 16 W=16 and 19% lower at W = 32 W=32 . W = 128 W=128 improves mean Best F1 by approximately 8% but with larger variance across datasets. Thus, W = 64 W=64 serves as a stable common setting rather than a per-dataset optimized choice.

sections.heading: V-A Univariate Results
sections.text: Table III shows that HCFM achieves the best result on every reported UCR metric, including best F1 of 0.742, AUROC of 0.922, AUPRC/AP of 0.757, and the lowest FP@95R of 0.171. Compared with the best non-HCFM baseline, DCDetector, HCFM improves best F1 from 0.672 to 0.742, corresponding to a 10.4% relative increase, and improves AUPRC/AP from 0.675 to 0.757, corresponding to a 12.1% relative increase. HCFM also improves VUS-PR from 0.651 to 0.694 and Hundman F1 from 0.692 to 0.776, while reducing FP@95R from 0.201 to 0.171, a 14.9% reduction in false positives at high recall. Among Flow-Matching-based baselines, FDM is the best non-HCFM variant. Relative to FDM, HCFM improves best F1 from 0.588 to 0.742, corresponding to a 26.2% relative increase, and improves AUPRC/AP from 0.594 to 0.757, corresponding to a 27.4% relative increase. HCFM also reduces FP@95R from 0.248 to 0.171, a 31.0% reduction. These gains reflect the advantage of component-specific divergence scoring: rather than estimating divergence over the full entangled vector field, HCFM concentrates the density-change signal in the compression head while retaining reverse-flow base-energy scoring. The comparison with vanilla FM isolates the value of compression-divergence evidence and structured field prediction. Vanilla FM uses data-space Conditional Flow Matching with a monolithic field and base-energy scoring. Relative to vanilla FM, HCFM improves best F1 from 0.562 to 0.742, corresponding to a 32.0% relative increase, improves AUPRC/AP from 0.566 to 0.757, corresponding to a 33.7% relative increase, and reduces FP@95R from 0.270 to 0.171, a 36.7% reduction. These improvements show that endpoint consistency alone is less informative than combining base energy with localized compression divergence.

sections.heading: V-B Main Results on Multivariate Benchmarks
sections.text: Table IV reports per-dataset multivariate results across GECCO, SWAN, MSL, SMAP, PSM, and SMD. HCFM achieves the best VUS-PR and best F1 on five of the six datasets, including GECCO, SWAN, MSL, SMAP, and PSM, while remaining competitive on SMD. For example, on GECCO, HCFM improves VUS-PR from 0.801 to 0.848 and best F1 from 0.841 to 0.881 over FDM, corresponding to relative gains of 5.9% and 4.8%, respectively. On PSM, HCFM improves VUS-PR from 0.856 to 0.888 and best F1 from 0.879 to 0.909 over FDM, corresponding to gains of 3.7% and 3.4%. The main exception is SMD, where Anomaly Transformer remains the best baseline with VUS-PR of 0.823 and best F1 of 0.860. HCFM remains competitive on this dataset, achieving VUS-PR of 0.812 and best F1 of 0.849, trailing Anomaly Transformer by 1.3% in VUS-PR and 1.3% in best F1. We conjecture that long-range temporal dependence may contribute to this small gap, but our analysis does not establish it as a causal explanation. Table V summarizes aggregate multivariate performance. HCFM achieves the best overall results, improving over the best non-HCFM aggregate baseline, Anomaly Transformer, from 0.901 to 0.914 in AUROC, from 0.744 to 0.768 in AUPRC/AP, and from 0.891 to 0.905 in Hundman F1. These correspond to relative improvements of 1.4%, 3.2%, and 1.6%, respectively. HCFM also reduces FP@95R from 0.514 to 0.486, a 5.4% reduction in false positives at high recall. Compared with the best Flow-Matching baseline, FDM, HCFM improves AUROC from 0.895 to 0.914, AUPRC/AP from 0.734 to 0.768, and Hundman F1 from 0.884 to 0.905, corresponding to relative gains of 2.1%, 4.6%, and 2.4%, respectively. HCFM also reduces FP@95R from 0.531 to 0.486, an 8.5% reduction. Overall, these results support the central claim of HCFM: structuring the Flow Matching vector field into divergence-free transport, density-changing compression, and lightweight residual components yields more informative anomaly scores than either Jacobian-free base-energy FM or monolithic divergence-based scoring.

sections.heading: VI Ablation Studies
sections.text: We ablate three design choices in HCFM: (i) whether compression-head divergence provides a more informative density-change signal than monolithic full-field divergence, (ii) whether the transport–compression–residual decomposition is responsible for the gains and (iii) whether residual scaling, residual-energy regularization, and orthogonality improve component allocation. Unless otherwise stated, all variants use the same preprocessing, window size, training budget, reverse ODE solver, and evaluation protocol as full HCFM, so differences in performance can be attributed to the ablated design choices rather than changes in the experimental setup.

sections.heading: VI-B Complementarity of Base Energy and Compression Divergence
sections.text: Figure 4 illustrates why combining base energy and compression divergence is useful. On UCR_45, base energy provides weak separation while compression divergence sharply localizes the anomaly. On UCR_21, base energy captures the anomalous interval more clearly than compression divergence. Thus, the two scores provide complementary anomaly evidence: base energy measures endpoint consistency with the nominal Gaussian base, while compression divergence captures localized density-changing deformation along the trajectory. Combining the two therefore allows HCFM to exploit both global deviation from the nominal base distribution and local deformation of the learned flow.

sections.heading: VI-C Structured Decomposition Versus Monolithic Fields

sections.heading: VII Conclusion and Future Work
sections.text: We introduced Helmholtz Component Flow Matching (HCFM), an unsupervised TSAD framework that addresses the entanglement of nominal transport and local density-changing behavior in monolithic FM predictors. HCFM parameterizes one final field through divergence-free transport, density-changing compression, and lightweight residual components, and combines reverse-flow base energy with compression-head divergence for complementary anomaly evidence. Experiments on 250 UCR datasets and six multivariate benchmarks show consistent gains over vanilla FM, FDM, and strong TSAD baselines, with improved detection quality and lower divergence-scoring cost. Ablations further show that the gains arise from the structured field parameterization rather than simply adding divergence: removing the compression head causes the largest degradation, while the transport and residual components also contribute to component allocation. More broadly, HCFM suggests component-structured parameterization as a design principle for Flow Matching when different vector-field roles require different constraints or diagnostics. Future work will explore incorporating attention mechanisms into the component-structured predictor, especially for multivariate time series with long-range temporal dependencies and cross-channel interactions. This could allow HCFM to retain its transport-compression decomposition while improving global context modeling.

Learn more × Back to arXiv License: arXiv.org perpetual non-exclusive license arXiv:2610.25059v1 [cs.LG] 18 Oct 2026 HCFM: Helmholtz Component Flow Matching for Time Series Anomaly Detection Shyam Sundar Saravanan Affiliation: Department of Computer Science Missouri University of Science and Technology Rolla, MO, USA ssdmw@mst.edu Tie Luo Affiliation: Department of ECE University of Kentucky Lexington, KY, USA t.luo@uky.edu Sanjay Madria Affiliation: Department of Computer Science Missouri University of Science and Technology Rolla, MO, USA madrias@mst.edu Abstract Flow Matching (FM) is an efficient simulation-free approach for training flow-based generative models, making it a promising foundation for scalable time-series anomaly detection (TSAD). However, standard FM learns a monolithic vector field in which nominal transport and local density-changing behavior are entangled. This creates a central challenge for TSAD; local expansion and contraction carry crucial anomaly-sensitive information, yet isolating this signal requires expensive Jacobian-trace estimation over the entire field. We propose Helmholtz Component Flow Matching (HCFM), an unsupervised TSAD framework that parameterizes the vector field prediction network with separate transport, compression, and residual heads. The transport head is constrained to be divergence-free, so divergence estimation is restricted to the compression head, while a lightweight residual head absorbs the remaining mismatch. This structured parameterization improves scalability and detection performance by separating volume-preserving nominal transport from density-changing compression, yielding cleaner anomaly signals from distinct deviations of nominal behavior. Experiments on large-scale univariate and multivariate TSAD benchmarks show that HCFM consistently improves detection accuracy while maintaining efficient inference compared with 16 baselines. The code is available at https://github.com/TrustAIoT/HCFM__time-series-anomaly/ Index Terms: time series, anomaly detection, generative modeling, flow matching, flow-based anomaly detection, vector-field decomposition, divergence-based scoring. I Introduction Time-series anomaly detection (TSAD) is commonly formulated as a one-class learning problem: a model is trained on nominal data and later scores future windows according to their deviation from learned normal behavior. This setting arises in industrial monitoring, cyber-physical systems, server telemetry, medical signals, spacecraft data, and other domains where anomalies are rare, costly, and difficult to label. Many deep TSAD methods therefore model nominality through reconstruction error, prediction error, likelihood, or latent-space distance [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 ] . A key challenge is that anomalies are not always expressed as large point-level error. Abnormal windows may instead appear through localized structural changes: suppressed variation, abnormal amplitude expansion, distorted morphology, or regime shifts that alter how nearby samples are distributed [ 6 , 7 ] . Such effects suggest that useful anomaly evidence may lie not only in how far a window is from nominal behavior, but also in how the learned nominal model locally deforms around it. However, most generative TSAD methods collapse these effects into a single reconstruction error, likelihood, or distance score, making it difficult to isolate the specific source of abnormality [ 5 ] . Flow Matching (FM) provides an appealing foundation for scalable TSAD. FM learns a vector field that transports samples from a simple base distribution to the data distribution using an efficient simulation-free objective [ 8 ] . This gives FM several practical advantages over common generative TSAD approaches: it avoids decoder reconstruction as the sole scoring mechanism, does not require iterative diffusion-style denoising, and does not impose the invertibility constraints of normalizing flows. These properties make FM attractive for efficient generative modeling of nominal time-series windows. However, standard FM predicts the vector field with a monolithic network, so nominal transport and local density-changing behavior are entangled in a single output. Divergence measures local expansion or contraction of the learned flow, and can therefore reveal anomaly-sensitive deformation around abnormal windows. Yet extracting this signal from standard FM requires estimating the Jacobian trace over the entire predicted field, which is computationally expensive and does not distinguish volume-preserving movement from density-changing behavior. Recent divergence-regularized FM methods, such as Flow Divergence Matching (FDM) [ 9 ] , recognize the importance of divergence by encouraging the learned field to better match the divergence of the target probability path. Nevertheless, FDM still applies divergence matching to a monolithic field predictor, so nominal transport and local expansion or contraction remain entangled in its output. We propose Helmholtz Component Flow Matching (HCFM), an unsupervised TSAD framework that parameterizes the FM field prediction with transport, compression, and residual heads. HCFM does not train separate flow models; rather, it predicts a single total vector field through an additive head structure. The transport head is constrained to be divergence-free, encouraging it to represent volume-preserving nominal movement. The compression head captures density-changing behavior through divergence, so divergence estimation is required only for this head rather than for the full predicted field. A lightweight residual head absorbs residual mismatch without dominating the transport and compression heads. Figure 1 illustrates the key idea. Standard FM uses a monolithic field that entangles nominal transport with local density-changing behavior. HCFM preserves a single final field but structures it into divergence-free transport, density-changing compression, and lightweight residual components. This component-structured parameterization localizes divergence-sensitive behavior to the compression head rather than the full field, preserving FM efficiency while exposing more interpretable anomaly evidence. We evaluate HCFM on large-scale univariate and multivariate TSAD benchmarks, including 250 UCR anomaly datasets and six multivariate datasets. Across these settings, HCFM improves over 16 representative baselines. On UCR, HCFM achieves a 10.4% relative best-F1 improvement over the best non-HCFM baseline, while on multivariate benchmarks it obtains the best aggregate results and the best per-dataset VUS-PR and best F1 on five of six datasets. HCFM also improves inference efficiency over monolithic divergence-based Flow Matching, reducing latency by 35% relative to FDM. These results show that component-structured Flow Matching yields more informative anomaly scores while maintaining efficient inference. In summary, our contributions are as follows: • Identify a structural limitation of monolithic Flow Matching for TSAD: nominal transport and local density-changing behavior are entangled in the learned vector field, making divergence-based anomaly evidence difficult to isolate. • Introduce HCFM, a component-structured Flow Matching framework that represents one final vector field through divergence-free transport, density-changing compression, and lightweight residual components, while retaining standard FM supervision. • Develop component-specific divergence scoring that localizes Jacobian-trace estimation to the compression component and combines this signal with reverse-flow base energy, yielding complementary evidence for different anomaly modes. • Establish the effectiveness and efficiency of the proposed structure through large-scale experiments on 250 UCR datasets and six multivariate benchmarks, including controlled ablations that isolate the contribution of field structure, divergence source, and residual allocation. • Open source code for reproducibility available at https://github.com/TrustAIoT/HCFM__time-series-anomaly/ Fig. 1: Motivating illustration of HCFM. (b) The transport head in HCFM is constrained to be divergence-free, encouraging volume-preserving nominal movement without local expansion or contraction. (c) HCFM predicts a single final vector field through additive transport, compression, and residual heads, v θ = v T + v C + v R v_{\theta}=v_{T}+v_{C}+v_{R} . This structured parameterization preserves a clean transport backbone while localizing density-changing behavior to the compression component and using the residual head to absorb residual mismatch. II Related Work II-A Time-Series Anomaly Detection Time-series anomaly detection (TSAD) spans industrial monitoring, cyber-physical systems, cloud infrastructure, healthcare, spacecraft telemetry, and scientific sensing. Classical approaches include statistical process control, autoregressive modeling, change-point detection, distance-based subsequence analysis, and matrix-profile methods [ 10 , 1 ] ; deep methods instead learn nominal temporal structure with recurrent, convolutional, graph-based, attention-based, and Transformer architectures [ 3 , 11 , 2 , 4 ] . Many deep detectors score by reconstruction or prediction error [ 3 , 12 , 11 , 4 ] , yet expressive decoders can reconstruct anomalies well and limited models over-penalize uncommon but valid nominal patterns. Anomaly Transformer [ 2 ] and TranAD [ 4 ] improve long-range dependency modeling, but stronger sequence modeling does not by itself distinguish global deviation, local expansion or contraction, and residual mismatch, which HCFM separates by structuring the generative vector-field predictor. II-B Generative Models and Flow Matching Generative detectors model nominal data and score deviations by likelihood, reconstruction, latent-space statistics, or transport. VAEs, GANs, normalizing flows, diffusion models, and score-based models have all been applied [ 13 , 14 , 15 , 16 , 17 , 5 ] , each with a characteristic tradeoff: VAEs and autoencoders inherit decoder-driven scoring artifacts [ 18 ] , GANs suffer mode collapse and training instability [ 19 ] , normalizing flows restrict architectures to maintain invertibility and tractable Jacobian determinants [ 20 ] , and diffusion models require iterative denoising or sampling. Flow Matching (FM) learns a vector field that transports a simple base distribution to the data distribution [ 8 , 21 ] , avoiding invertibility constraints, iterative diffusion-style denoising, and sole reliance on reconstruction. Standard FM, however, predicts the field with a monolithic output that couples nominal transport with local density change, making expansion or contraction difficult to isolate as an anomaly signal. Recent time-series FM work includes TSFlow [ 22 ] , which adapts FM to probabilistic forecasting using Gaussian-process priors and optimal-transport couplings. Closer to our setting, SGFM [ 23 ] applies conditional FM to TSAD with state-space sequence modeling, but still predicts a monolithic field. HCFM instead structures the learned vector field itself into transport, compression, and residual components, so that volume-preserving transport and density-changing behavior provide distinct anomaly signals. II-C Divergence Matching and Divergence-Free Flows Divergence measures the local expansion or contraction of a continuous-time vector field and governs density evolution along the flow. Flow Divergence Matching (FDM) [ 9 ] trains the field to match both the target vector field and the divergence of the target probability path, addressing density information that directional matching alone may not capture. However, FDM retains a monolithic field in which transport and density change remain coupled. Divergence-free continuous flows [ 24 ] are volume-preserving normalizing flows: zero divergence gives incompressible dynamics with unit Jacobian determinant magnitude and simplifies quantities such as differential entropy, but constraining the entire flow prevents it from modeling arbitrary density changes. HCFM instead predicts a single FM field through additive heads and applies the constraint selectively: a divergence-free transport head preserves volume, a compression head captures density change and supplies component-specific divergence as anomaly evidence, and a residual head absorbs the remaining mismatch. II-D Positioning of This Work HCFM differs from prior FM-based TSAD primarily in how the vector field is parameterized and diagnosed. It retains a single final field and standard FM supervision, but separates divergence-free transport, density-changing compression, and residual mismatch. Relative to standard FM, it exposes expansion and contraction through a dedicated compression component; relative to FDM, it localizes divergence scoring to that component; and unlike fully divergence-free flows, it preserves density-changing capacity in the overall model. Thus, HCFM provides a component-structured parameterization of Flow Matching for separating nominal transport from density-changing behavior and enabling targeted derivative-based diagnostics. Fig. 2: Architecture of Helmholtz Component Flow Matching (HCFM). HCFM trains a data-space Flow Matching model over interpolated time-series windows and replaces a monolithic vector-field predictor with additive transport, compression, and residual heads. The transport head captures divergence-free nominal movement, the compression head provides localized density-changing evidence through component-specific divergence, and the residual head absorbs remaining mismatch while being kept lightweight. Training supervises the combined final field and uses residual-energy and orthogonality regularization to shape the internal component allocation. At inference, HCFM combines base-energy and compression-divergence for anomaly detection and localization. For the univariate setting, we use the UCR Time Series Anomaly Archive [ 25 ] . The UCR benchmark contains 250 curated time series from diverse real-world domains. Each dataset consists of a nominal training segment and a test segment containing an annotated anomalous interval. The benchmark includes point, contextual, and collective anomaly patterns, making it a challenging testbed for one-class TSAD. Prior work has noted that many TSAD benchmarks contain annotation errors, trivial anomalies, or unrealistic anomaly densities [ 26 ] ; UCR was designed to mitigate many of these issues and provides a more reliable evaluation environment. Multivariate benchmarks. For the multivariate setting, we use six widely adopted real-world TSAD benchmarks. SMAP and MSL contain spacecraft telemetry from NASA missions [ 1 ] ; PSM and SMD contain server and infrastructure monitoring signals [ 27 , 3 ] ; GECCO contains water-quality measurements from a distribution monitoring system [ 28 ] ; and SWAN contains space-weather monitoring signals [ 29 ] . These datasets contain multichannel time series with ground-truth anomaly intervals and cover diverse operational conditions, anomaly densities, and inter-channel dependencies. IV-B Baselines and Variants We compare HCFM against representative reconstruction-based, Transformer-based, diffusion-based, contrastive, and flow-based baselines. For reconstruction-based detection, we compare against established baselines such as LSTM-AE, DENSE-AE, LSTM-DT, USAD [ 11 ] , OmniAnomaly [ 3 ] , DONUT [ 30 ] , TadGAN [ 12 ] , and TSI-GAN [ 18 ] , where applicable. We additionally include MERLIN [ 31 ] , a discord-based time-series anomaly detection baseline. For Transformer-based detection, we include TranAD [ 4 ] and Anomaly Transformer [ 2 ] . We also compare against recent diffusion- and contrastive-learning baselines, including DiffAD [ 32 ] , ImDiffusion [ 33 ] , DCDetector [ 34 ] , and CARLA [ 35 ] . For flow-based baselines, we include vanilla data-space Flow Matching, Flow Divergence Matching (FDM), and SGFM [ 23 ] . Vanilla FM uses the same data-space Conditional Flow Matching objective as HCFM, but predicts the vector field with a monolithic network. FDM incorporates divergence information into a monolithic FM predictor. SGFM is a recent Flow-Matching-based TSAD method that combines conditional Flow Matching with state-space sequence modeling. These baselines isolate whether HCFM’s gains arise from Flow Matching itself, from divergence information alone, from sequence-modeling improvements in prior FM-based TSAD, or from the proposed component-wise field parameterization. For HCFM, the final model uses the transport, compression, and residual heads described in Sec. III-C . The main score family combines reverse-flow base energy with compression-head divergence.
